Okay, so I need to figure out the volume in milliliters of 0.312 kg of Freon-12 when placed at the bottom of the Marianas Trench. The problem is asking for the volume, so I know I need to use the density of Freon-12 under those conditions. 

First, I remember that the Marianas Trench is super deep, about 11,000 meters, which is 1100 atmospheres of pressure. The temperature there is pretty cold, around 1-4 degrees Celsius. Freon-12, also known as dichlorodifluoromethane, is a refrigerant, so I think its density might change with pressure and temperature.

I tried to look up the density of Freon-12 at high pressure and low temperature, but the search didn't give me the exact numbers I needed. The results mentioned a PDF document about its thermodynamic properties, but I couldn't access it. Without the density, I can't calculate the volume.

So, I made an assumption. I found the standard density of Freon-12 at room temperature and atmospheric pressure, which is about 1.486 g/cm³. I figured that at 1100 atm, the pressure would make the density much higher. I estimated a 15% increase, so the density would be around 1.7099 g/cm³.

Next, I converted the mass from kilograms to grams: 0.312 kg is 312 grams. Then, using the formula Volume = Mass / Density, I plugged in the numbers. 312 grams divided by 1.7099 g/cm³ gives me about 182.5 cm³, which is 182.5 milliliters. Rounding that to the nearest whole number, I got 183 mL.

I think this is a reasonable estimate, but I'm not entirely sure if the 15% increase is accurate. Maybe the density change isn't linear with pressure, but without the exact data, I had to make an educated guess. I hope this estimate is close enough for the problem's purposes.
